title: Determination of Attainment by the Attainment Date; California; Mariposa County; 2015 8-Hour Ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards
summary:
Here’s the headline: three federal rules just landed that affect work authorization, local air quality planning in California, and how a new bio-based pesticide can be used on food.

First, the Department of Homeland Security changed how renewals of employment authorization cards work. For renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025, simply applying will no longer automatically extend a worker’s permission to work, unless another law or a specific notice says otherwise, including some cases tied to Temporary Protected Status. This gives employers clearer cutoffs and may reduce confusion about expired cards. But it could create work gaps for noncitizen employees if renewals aren’t approved before the card expires, and add pressure on human resources teams to plan earlier and manage verification risks.

Second, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized that Mariposa County, California met the 2015 national ozone standard by its August 3, 2024 deadline. The finding relies on complete, certified data from 2021–2023, with days affected by major wildfires removed under long-standing “exceptional event” rules. As a result, the area no longer has to carry extra “backup” measures for missing the target, which eases some planning burdens. Residents and visitors benefit from the confirmation that local air met the standard over that period. On the other hand, the area is not being redesignated to full attainment, so other obligations remain. Some may also question excluding wildfire-driven spikes given how often smoke now affects air quality.

Third, the agency granted a tolerance exemption for a polypeptide pesticide ingredient from Biotalys NV, meaning there is no need to set a maximum residue limit on foods and animal feed when it’s used as directed and with good agricultural practices. This opens the door for farmers and food producers to use another tool, potentially speeding up adoption of a bio-based product and simplifying residue compliance. Consumers could see more options framed as lower-residue or bio-derived. At the same time, advocates may ask for continued monitoring of real-world use, especially for children’s exposure, and competing manufacturers may feel market pressure as exemptions can reduce regulatory hurdles for new entrants.

In short, workers and employers should prepare earlier for work card renewals, Mariposa County gets recognition for meeting the ozone mark without a full regulatory reset, and agriculture gains a new pest control option with fewer residue constraints—each change offering benefits to some while raising practical questions for others.
